sentences.text: Hi, Jack, how you doing?
Good, how are you?
Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
Good, good.
Give me one second here.
We're joined by at least three AIs.
At least.
@ least.
Yes.
Yeah, I think there's.
I think there are three.
Yes.
I don't know who's all of them are.
One of them's definitely mine and one's definitely yours.
So that's.
Yeah.
I don't know what close and Firefly.
Is, but mine is Fireplace is me.
Yeah.
Okay.
I don't know what close is.
That doesn't look familiar.
This is our CRM, but that's the first time I've seen it invite itself, which is interesting.
Okay.
One of my team has put in a request so they can see the meeting afterwards.
But anyway.
Well, thank you for joining.
And where are you based?
I'm based in the US in the Los Angeles area, so Valencia, California.
Valencia, California.
Oh, brilliant.
Yeah, it's northern LA county.
Are you stateside?
Are you in the UK where?
I'm in the UK.
I was actually.
We lived in Los Angeles in 23 for six months.
Oh, you did?
Which part?
We were on Manhattan Beach.
Oh, that's really nice.
Yeah, The South Bay area.
Yeah, it's beautiful.
And our offices are based there as well, so we've got.
Most of our team actually is US based, but we are HQ'd in London.
I'm the founder of the business, so.
Okay, we've got a completely international business.
I think we've got companies listed currently from Switzerland and Hong Kong and Australia, the US the UK.
But US, I would say, makes up probably about 95% of our business.
All right.
So I know LA fairly well.
We're there quite a lot.
Okay, good.
You are, you're looking to.
To sell.
It says on the.
The note that you sent Dell merge roll up.
Something in that universe.
Yes.
Okay, well, let's.
Let's figure it out.
So I'll tell you a little bit about us and then let's get into.
Into you.
So we're an M and A advisory called Capital A.
We work with the buy and the sell side.

We have a, a sell side platform called Agencies Co and on the buy side we work with agency owners that are looking to grow or we work with private equity or private investors as well, helping them to find agencies to buy and then help them with the entire process.
So these calls really just get to know and see where you're at and if we can help you and then maybe we can set up a second call and get things really Moving.
So it'd be good to hear a little bit Jack about your business and what you've built and what it is that you're looking to do or what your options seem to be.
See how we can help you.
Okay, sure.
So let me start first by saying, is there, by asking really, is there a minimum deal size that you look for in the size of an agency?
So we work right across the boards.
We work with agencies that are doing a couple of hundred thousand, all the way up to agencies that are doing a couple hundred million.
So.
Okay, we're right across the board in that sense.
And you'd be surprised actually, Jack.
A lot of buyers there is a sweet spot that's at the lower end of the market.
So if you're an agency that's sub $1 million revenue, there's still a ton of buyers and a lot of interest in the smaller agencies as well.
Yeah.
So we currently are sub 1 million.
We're in the 800k range right now.
The last few years, at one point, at our peak, we were at 2.3 million.
Back in 2018, Covid hit.
We lost a major client right before COVID hit.
And we've never really grown back to where we were.
And I've kept it going for the last five years.
But at some point I have to recognize that it would probably be better to grow through acquisition or merger, meaning being acquired or being merged into a larger organization or cashing out.
But I'm not ready to retire yet.
I would like to work.
I'd like to work another 10 years, you know.
Yeah, I'm 61 years old and I'm very healthy and I have plenty of.
Plenty of juice.
Yeah, you don't look 60 at all.
Oh, well, thank you.
I appreciate that.
I try.
Thank you.
So what is the core stuff?
I can see you're an E commerce agency.
What's like the typical services that you sell to clients.
So a lot of them come to us for the more complex technical issues, the system integration issues, data migration, platform migrations.
Those are the typical things.
Someone's on some bespoke platform and they want to move to Shopify or they want to move to BigCommerce or they want something along lines.
Lines or they want to integrate with, you know, an ERP system, that type of thing.
But we also do complete web design development, all the front end work, all the project management, all the testing.
And then the thing that keeps us going that a lot of other agencies don't do is we have maintenance and support.
So Those are retainers, I would say.
Probably do about 250k a year right now just in maintenance and support.
And the rest would be projects and some software licensing.
Right.
So what does a typical client look like and how much do you charge for your services?
Typical.
Let me just pull some things up so I can remember what.
Some of them aren't as typical as others, but it's a bit of a mix of some clients that are on legacy platforms.
For example, when we started out we did mostly back in 2010 we were doing mostly large scale websites on a content management solution called Net Nuke or dnn.
We still have a few clients that are on that platform where we're doing some project work.

When we're doing maintenance work, it's typically a mid market client or a nonprofit organ and occasionally a government, more like a military government project though we haven't done much of that in the last few years.
Wasn't that built on ASP first before.
They ported it to net.net new you mean or.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
It actually first came out in 2001 when Microsoft introduced the.
NET framework.
I did it.
Was it okay?
Yeah, and it was, it was.
It was an open source project that many people contributed to and it was highly recognized as a great reference implementation.
And then they, they kind of spawned it off and turned it into a business and then they got funded and eventually acquired by private equity.
So it is still going as a platform, is it dnn?
It is.
They haven't done much with it.
They're mostly just.
The private equity is mostly just milking the existing clients and increasing the price 25% every time at renewal.
So are you just moving clients off that onto other more popular or more modern platforms?
Yes, we've moved clients onto Shopify, we're moving clients onto WordPress.
We are doing some other types of custom implementations.
We also, we've done some projects where people came to us specifically because they wanted to migrate their E commerce platform from something to something older to something more modern.
And so I guess people are just coming to you because they have an E commerce business.
It's not that you're in any particular verticals.
So they may not specifically have an E commerce business.
They may have a business that has an E commerce component to it.
But E commerce is not the only thing that they do.
As far as verticals, we for many years were not vertically focused.
We were just, you know, everything was well, we hear your experts in this or that.
And it was all partner referral based or client referral.
Based, which is, you know, a way to grow organically, but hard to really, really scale.

We are, we're becoming more vertically focused because Shopify invited us to participate in their Shopify Plus Partner program, which requires not only jumping through some hoops as far as certifications and trainings, but bringing a certain number of leads.
And we've chosen to be more vertically focused in order to acquire some more business.
So right now we're focusing on the pet nutrition industry for a number of reasons.
First of all, it's the.
One of the fastest growing industries right now, and it's less likely to be subject to tariffs, which everybody's concerned about right now, because it's a, it's a food product.
It has an expiration date if it's in the U.S.
most of the products are either made in the U.S.
which you're allowed to say if some of your ingredients are sourced from other countries, or they're made and sourced in the US which is a larger percentage of them.
Okay, so smart move then.
So it's a pretty stable business going forward.
Thank you.
Thank you.
And we do have, you know, some case studies working with the Mars Corporation for their Wisca and Pedigree brands, so at least we have some credibility in that domain.
Yeah.
Okay, brilliant.
All right, that's really interesting.
And so what are you looking to do?
You, you said you want to, you want to carry on work for the next 10 years.
Are you just looking to get acquired into a larger business just to make your life easier?
You know, in terms of, like, having to find everybody's wages every month that comes with that?
Or is, is there, there's something else, like a lifestyle change or, or something.
I wouldn't say a lifestyle change.
I would say it's more the latter.
Not the latter, the former.
Which is, you know, I, I want to take the, the cash flow headache that I want.
I don't want to wear the CFO hat anymore.
I'm very good at sales, account management, product delivery, managing people.
I want to do the things that I like to do that I do well, that.
Where I can provide the most value and not be distracted by those other things and not carry the liabilities on the books.
You know, that that's just as you can imagine, it's a stressful situation, of.
Course, and you just want to do the work that you're, you're passionate about, which I totally understand.
Yes.
Financially, is there a number that you're, you're trying to get to?
What's, what's your thoughts there well, I've.
Had a lot of thoughts about it and I've had a lot of conversations about it.
I've heard different things, like 2 to 4 times EBITDA, 3 to 5 times EBITDA, 0.8 to 1.2 gross.
Those are the different numbers that I've heard in the industry.
So ideally, if we can, if we can get the adjusted EBITDA, we're about 24%.
I run a lot of personal expenses through the business.
We could probably adjust it to more, closer to 30%.
So if we can get around a million, that would be ideal.
Okay, so 1, 1 million in total.
So, yeah, I mean, you're, you're, you're not wrong.
I think, you know, generally speaking, most agencies sell somewhere between a four to six times multiple.
Smaller agencies obviously could be less, but it really does depend on what your area of focus is, you know, the vertical that you're in and just whether somebody really needs an agency of that type.
On the day that we're marketing, what we tend to do is go to market with a multiple already.
And so we, we advertise a price.
But what does happen is most buyers have their own formula for coming up with how they're going to pay for it and what they're looking to pay.
They want to pay as little as possible, I'm sure.
Yeah, sometimes, sometimes we've actually had people pay way more than we've asked for.
When, you know, we've got into negotiation, they've seen a piece of kit that they really want, they're willing to pay more for it.
So.
But yeah, as you can imagine, most people want to spend less than you're asking for.
So really negotiation, and that's where we really come in to help you get the best valuation for your business.
So we've got a few ways of working together.
What we, we're looking to do really is get you listed on our agencies platform.
So agencies is a platform for agency owners who are looking to sell.
We have a lot of sort of organic traffic that visits the site, but we also have a mailing list of about 20,000 marketing agencies as well.
And what we're looking to do, particularly with the large businesses, we spend quite a lot of time building bespoke lists of buyers that we, we also market to.
But I would imagine that there's probably two packages that are going to work better for you.
So we have a sort of seller package that we, we prepare you to go to market for.
And it's really for, it's targeted at businesses that aren't quite doing 1 million in revenue.
But we do take 5% on the deal as well.
So when we get a deal closed, we take a 5% win fee.
So it's.

And what we're looking for that is to give you a full valuation and listing and your marketing materials to get you live on the agency's platform and get you marketed to our 20,000 marketing agency buyers on our mailing list.
Okay, Is that something that you would be in the market for or what's your thoughts?
Well, so I like your fees.
Your fees are very competitive.
I have a couple of questions on the types of deals that you think would be a potential.
Because one of the things I'm not interested in is an earn out.
Because.
I've seen too many times or you know, they find a way for the founder to not get their earn out.
You know, you don't really have control over it as much.
I'd much rather carry a note or, you know, for example, they don't want to pay all cash.
I'd rather carry a note over five years or do some kind of a portion of it in equity of the acquiring entity.
Yeah, seeing those kinds of deals.
Yeah, those deals happen particularly at the lower end of the market.
I mean, it really does depend on who the buyer is.
The earnouts are very typical.

But of course, if you have a valuation on, on day one that you're selling the business for and then somebody messes you around for three years and doesn't give you the rest of the money, you're basically selling it for half the price that you've agreed to.
In my experience, that doesn't happen a lot.
But you hear about these stories more often than you hear about the easy good ones, because obviously people have got a gripe and they're talking about it.
So I think deals tend to go through smoothly and certainly the ones that we work on because our fees are based on the payment structures as well.

But the smaller deals, you are able to negotiate the seller's note and also if we've got an owner operator who wants to buy the business, so say they're getting an SBA loan and they're looking to buy the business and then operate it themselves, they tend to to be more open to that.
Small sellers know most of the cash up front.

But I've got to say what tends to happen, and this is because the SBA actually have previously made it a rule, but I think they're a bit more lax on it now, but they ask for the, the owner to step out of the business on day one.
So you're, you're sometimes retained as a consultant for like a year.
So I, I'm not.

I mean, given that you want to stay in the business for 10 years, it may be that if you want to get that assurity to get the rest of the money out of the deal, then you might not be kept on for as long.
And if you were to work in ear now, you might become part of a much bigger business for a much longer period of time where you could stay in for 10 years.
So.
And 10 years is.
It doesn't have to be 10 years.
Right.
It could be three years, it could be five years.

I just don't want to exit and then to go look for a job in a field that I'm not interested in or, you know, and ageism is a thing as well, even though, you know, I know, I think I could probably get past that.
But.
Yeah, Yeah.
I mean, the idea of just selling to an individual entrepreneur that wants to do what I do, I'm a little skeptical about doing that because.
Yeah, I mean, they're, they're, they're gonna, I just feel that that's not gonna be, you know, they're gonna find a way for me to, to exit and just maybe keep me on with the consulting fee and.
Yeah, I mean, if that's the only opportunity that's out there, I guess I have to consider it, but it wouldn't be much.
Yeah.
So I appreciate that.
And it's always good to get feedback.
Excuse me, from the seller.
We don't have tons of those types of buyers in on our mailing list anyway, so.
They do, they do come along.
Ideally, we'll find somebody that's looking to keep you in the business for the amount of time you want to stay on.
And if we can get the seller's note and everything's structured how you would like it, then, then that's the best scenario.
What tends to happen is we get totally different types of buyers and usually it's sort of three, four, five different types of buyers.
They're all completely different from one another.
So you just get to pick which type of buyer you want to work with.
And what we do find, particularly with Californian listings, is that we get a lot of interest, particularly in the small listings as well.
So I should imagine you'll probably get two or three at least offers on the table within the first sort of three or four months.
Okay.
What are you usually seeing in terms of a timeline, I won't quote you on this and I know we're recording, but I still, I understand.
What are you seeing in this market for these types of deals in terms of how long they're taking?
Yeah, so we, we have a six month process and most of our deals get done within that.
We do have some that run longer and of course there's always the odd listing that just doesn't get sold.
We're, we're running a six month process.
So start to finish.
How that looks is like the first month takes us to get set up.
The months two and three, we're having a lot of meetings, maybe even more than two, two or three a week.
By the end of month three or it depends, you know, if it's been a bit thin on the ground, we get to month four.
But we, we put a line in the sand and ask for offers by a certain date.
And then once we have that offer it usually with a smaller listing as well, it takes about 30, just over 30 days to do due diligence and legals and get the deal closed.
So end to end it usually ends up being about six months.
We did sell a smaller agency in Los Angeles last year and to my memory it was about four and a half months start to finish.
It was really quick.
It got 45 signed NDAs within 24 hours.
So he had a lot of interest.
He had five offers and was able to just pick who wanted to work with.
How big was he?
Tiny 5 or 600,000 revenue, something like that.
Interesting.
And this was recently?
Yep, last year.
Yeah.
If you want to look on, I'll send you case studies document after.
And on that case that is documented, say a guy called Arjun.
So you can, there's a video there, you can watch his story.
Okay, so if I was to carry a note, what's the typical interest and length of time and or percentage of the, the deal that you're seeing?
Yeah, usually it's just whatever the base, the base rate is for the interest usually over a three year period.
Three year?
Yeah, so say like 5% on the, on whatever it is over a three year period.
Okay.
Now is, are your fees based on post sale equity or just the, or the seller note or is it, is it just strictly that initial transaction?
So we prefer to take it on the transaction.
It's actually 10% usually on, on deals that are less than 1 million.
I can send you everything over.
But we take the money when our clients take the money.
That's how most of our clients prefer to.
To have the deal.
But some, some of our clients have bought us out on day one.
And usually that's because they know they're going to smash the targets and, and earn way more.
And in those scenarios, they've just said, look, we're going to give you all of the money on day one.
And we're fine with that because it means we don't have to wait around for three years.
So.
Right, so if it was all cash, it would be 5%.
If it was a equity, if it was a note and cash, it would be 10%.
No, it doesn't really make a difference how.
It's.
It's just on, on size.
Okay, but earlier you had said 5%.
You just.
I did, yeah.
I did, but, yeah, sorry.
So it's, it's 10 on, on valuations that are less than 1 million.
So we'd have to look at what the deal looked like if the.
I mean, obviously, I don't know what all your numbers are right now.
If the deal came in and it was, you know, 1.2 million, then it's 5% under a million.
We charge 10 on the deal just because our team, you know, it's a professional M and A team and we want them to be motivated to close the smaller deals, too, so.
Of course.
Yeah, I understand that.
Let me just think.
What else did I want to.
What would happen if I brought the buyer?
Would that change anything?
Yeah, so.
So if you brought the buyer, we've got, like, a tiered approach to that, so I, I can show you what that looks like.
Okay.
But.
But we would take a smaller percentage on the deal.

If you brought the buyer in and you wanted us to negotiate the deal, if you found your own buyer, you wanted to just negotiate yourself, then we're also happy stepping away and letting you get the deal done on your own.
Yeah, I mean, I would rather not negotiate it myself because, you know, it takes the emotion out of the negotiation.
Yeah, exactly.
Yeah.
I mean, it's a very emotional experience regardless.
Yeah, of course.
And we, we can work in that capacity as well.
So if you were to bring a buyer in, we could, we could just take a low percentage for our win fee, which is fine.
Yeah.
Okay.
So it would be 25% up front for the valuation, 10% on the back end.
Is that right?
Sorry, 25% on the valuation is $2,500.
I meant, I'm sorry, 2500.
If I said 25%, I misspoke.
Yes.
We wouldn't be talking.
Yeah, I take 25%, day one.
No, 2500, you're correct.
Yeah, that's so just because you're a smaller business, we have as frictionless fees as possible to get you on the site and listed.
Yeah, we do have competitors that charge the same for large and small businesses, but it just prices everybody out of being able to get a transaction done.
Okay, I'm trying to think if I have any other questions or if you.
Have any other questions for me, I've got another call.
But you know what, I will send you everything on email after this.
And of course, Jack, if you do have any more questions, then let's hop onto a second call and we can go through everything that you need answering on that call.
But it's, it's a pretty painless sign up process with us.
And then we just want to get you listed and marketed to our mailing list as quickly as possible.
And we can get a deal done in way less than six months with a smaller business.
So one last question.
The $2,500, is that applied at the end, toward the back end, is that credited?
So it's netted off.
However, we have a minimum fee target to get to as well.
So all of that really depends on the value of the deal.
Yeah, but, but we have a minimum 50k fee.
So if, if the, the deal is worth 500k, it would be, it wouldn't be, it would be the 50k minimum.
However, if the deal is worth 750k, it would be netted out.
Yes.
Okay.
All right, great.
All right, thank you.
I appreciate it.
I'll look for your email.
All right, brilliant.
Good to meet you, Jack.
Enjoy the rest of your day.

summary.overview: In the Sales/Business Development Meeting, Jack Kurtz and Andy Day introduced their respective backgrounds, with Jack representing an e-commerce agency and Andy being the founder of Capital A, an M&A advisory firm. Jack discussed his agency's focus on complex technical issues, especially within the pet nutrition sector, and revealed an annual revenue of approximately $800k, aiming for a $1 million business valuation. Andy explained the typical sales process and fee structure, noting that most agencies sell for a multiple of 4-6 times their EBITDA. Jack expressed a preference for seller's notes or equity arrangements over earnouts and emphasized the desire for Capital A to manage negotiations to minimize emotional involvement. Action items were established, with Andy agreeing to send Jack relevant documentation and Jack planning to review the information for potential follow-up discussions.
summary.short_summary: In a Sales/Business Development meeting, Jack Kurtz, representing an e-commerce agency, and Andy Day, founder of Capital A, an M&A advisory firm, shared insights on agency valuation and sales processes. Jack highlighted his agency's specialization in complex technical issues within the pet nutrition sector, revealing an annual revenue of approximately $800k, with a goal of achieving a $1 million valuation. Andy outlined the typical sales process for agencies, noting that they often sell for a multiple of 4-6 times their EBITDA, and discussed Capital A's fee structure, which includes a seller package for $2,500 plus a success fee. Jack expressed a preference for seller's notes or equity arrangements over earnouts and emphasized the importance of having Capital A manage negotiations to reduce emotional involvement. Action items included Andy sending documentation to Jack for further discussion.
